name: Lenticulostriate arteries
summary: A fan of small perforating arteries that rise from the first segment of the middle cerebral artery (lateral lenticulostriates) and from the proximal anterior cerebral artery (medial lenticulostriates, including the recurrent artery of Heubner), pierce the anterior perforated substance and supply the putamen, globus pallidus, caudate and the internal capsule. They are end arteries, so their occlusion produces lacunar infarcts and their rupture under chronic hypertension produces the typical deep putaminal hemorrhage.

anatomy.location: Arise from the superior and posterior wall of the M1 segment (and from A1 for the medial group) in the Sylvian cistern, ascend through the anterior perforated substance, and fan out through the lentiform nucleus toward the body of the caudate and the genu and anterior part of the posterior limb of the internal capsule.

subdivisions.name: Medial lenticulostriates (including Heubner's artery)
subdivisions.note: head of the caudate, anterior limb of the internal capsule, anterior putamen

subdivisions.name: Lateral lenticulostriates
subdivisions.note: putamen, lateral globus pallidus, body of the caudate, genu and superior posterior limb of the internal capsule

function: Supply the striatum, the globus pallidus and the corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers travelling in the genu and posterior limb of the internal capsule.

bestView.label: perforators rising through the anterior perforated substance into the lentiform nucleus
putamen and internal capsule, the lacune and hypertensive hemorrhage site

imaging.normalAppearance: Individual vessels are below MRI resolution but can be seen as fine radiating lines on CTA and 7 T imaging. Their territory is the lentiform nucleus, caudate and internal capsule on axial slices at the level of the frontal horns.

pathology.finding: A small (under 15–20 mm) focus of restricted diffusion in the putamen, internal capsule or corona radiata; older lacunes become CSF-signal cavities with a FLAIR rim.
pathology.timing: DWI positive acutely; cavitation over weeks to months

pathology.finding: Hyperdense hematoma centered on the putamen, spreading medially into the internal capsule or rupturing into the lateral ventricle; surrounding hypodense edema grows over days.
pathology.timing: Hyperdense immediately; isodense after ~1–2 weeks; hypodense chronically

pathology.finding: A comma-shaped infarct of the whole lenticulostriate territory when M1 is transiently occluded and the cortex is saved by collaterals.

imaging.sequenceOfChoice: DWI for lacunes; non-contrast CT for hemorrhage; SWI shows old microbleeds in the same territory

lesionEffects.deficit: Pure motor hemiparesis (face, arm and leg equally)
lesionEffects.mechanism: Corticospinal and corticobulbar fibers in the posterior limb and genu of the internal capsule

lesionEffects.deficit: Dense hemiplegia with gaze deviation and decreased consciousness
lesionEffects.mechanism: Large putaminal hemorrhage with capsular involvement and mass effect

examination: Check that face, arm and leg are affected to a similar degree with no cortical signs
Look for hemiballismus or dystonia after recovery
Measure blood pressure and look for retinal hypertensive change
pearls: A hemiparesis that is equal in face, arm and leg with no aphasia, neglect or field cut is capsular, not cortical
The lenticulostriates are the classic site of hypertensive hemorrhage because they leave a large trunk at right angles and bear its full pressure

pitfalls: Small deep infarcts can also come from emboli or from M1 atheroma occluding the perforator origins, so cardiac and large-vessel evaluation is still needed
